Trump Demands a "350 Billion Dollar" Military Bill Before Democrats Take Over. Palantir Has a Stake ©@dotshock via Canva, @dotshock via Canva
Key Takeaways

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) could benefit from President Donald Trump's push for an additional $350 billion in military spending before Democrats take control of Congress.

Senate appropriators proposed nearly $1.1 trillion in defense spending on November 16, incorporating approximately $69 billion in priorities originally sought through reconciliation.

Palantir's U.S. government revenue surged 96% to $953 million in the third quarter, while U.S. commercial revenue grew 148% to $984 million.

Palantir trades at roughly 75x forward earnings, making it a stock I would avoid buying at its current valuation despite its exceptional growth.

President Donald Trump wants Congress to approve an additional $350 billion in military spending before Democrats take control in January.

That could create new opportunities for Palantir, whose artificial intelligence software is gaining traction across the federal government. But the money remains uncertain, and Palantir's premium valuation leaves little room for delays in turning military spending into revenue.

Trump Wants $350 Billion Before January

On November 12, Trump urged Senate Republican leaders to move quickly on a military reconciliation bill before Democrats assume control of Congress.

In his Truth Social post, Trump called on Senate leadership to "IMMEDIATELY move on the 350 Billion Dollar Reconciliation Bill."

The administration's broader $1.5 trillion defense request includes substantial funding for autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, munitions, and Golden Dome missile defense.

Those priorities align with Palantir's government-focused software business, although the company has not been guaranteed any portion of the proposed spending.

The situation changed on November 16, when Senate appropriators unveiled a nearly $1.1 trillion defense spending proposal.

According to Breaking Defense, the proposal incorporates nearly $69 billion in priorities originally sought through reconciliation into the regular defense budget.

That provides another potential funding route for selected military programs, but it does not guarantee new contracts for Palantir.

For shareholders, the key question is how much approved military spending ultimately becomes revenue for the company.

The British government has opted to keep Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) in charge of a key National Health Service data project for another three years, putting off an earlier opportunity to end the relationship.

The decision leaves the U.S. software company in place until 2029. Officials plan to start looking for competing providers next summer, giving British technology businesses an opportunity to pursue the work.

The arrangement comes amid political pressure over Palantir's access to sensitive health information. Some lawmakers have questioned whether the company should manage NHS data, while domestic technology firms have been viewed as potential alternatives.

Palantir won the 330 million ($440 million) agreement in 2023. Its Federated Data Platform went live the following year, helping NHS services organize information and manage hospital waiting lists.

The original contract was due to run through 2031, but the government's decision not to trigger an early exit means the next major test for Palantir will come when the work goes out to competition in 2029.

6 Big Funds Sold Palo Alto Networks Last Quarter. Should You Follow Them Before Earnings? ©@jittawit21 from jittawit21 via Canva, @BlackJack3D from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Six big funds, including Gavin Baker's Atreides Management, cut their Palo Alto Networks stakes by 20% to 94% in the third quarter, and the stock is down 20% since Sept. 30.

Five of the six still held Palo Alto positions worth 2% or more of their 13F stocks at Sept. 30.

At about 76x forward earnings, Palo Alto costs more than Palantir and three times as much as Microsoft, while management guides to 8% to 9% EPS growth this fiscal year.

On price, the sellers look right, and I wouldn't buy before the Nov. 18 report shows per-share earnings catching up.

Six big funds cut their stakes in Palo Alto Networks (PANW:NASDAQ) in the third quarter. That's what their 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30 show, filed between Nov. 5 and Nov. 16. The stock is down 20% from its Sept. 30 close, and Palo Alto reports its fiscal first quarter on Nov. 18.

Most of them still own plenty

None of the six sold out completely. The cuts ranged from a fifth of the stake to nearly all of it:

Source: each fund's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026. Size is what the firm manages, except for Kranot, Triodos and LGT, where it's what their 13Fs hold in US stocks.

LGT came closest to leaving, with just 6,678 shares left. Triodos sits at the other end: it trimmed 20%, and Palo Alto was still its largest holding. Gavin Baker's Atreides cut its stake by a third, to 578,905 shares. A 13F only shows what a fund held on the last day of the quarter, so we don't know when these funds sold, what they got, or why.

The same funds pay a lot less for Microsoft

Five of the six also own Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), and for some it's a much bigger position. It was Mirova's No. 2 holding at 6.3% of its 13F stocks, and LGT's No. 3 at 8.2%. Four of the five trimmed it too, by 7% to 28%. Atreides went the other way and opened a new Microsoft position of 275,976 shares, worth $142 million. Microsoft trades at about 25x forward earnings, a third of Palo Alto's multiple, and it's up 1% since Sept. 30.

Palo Alto even costs more than Palantir (PLTR:NASDAQ) on forward earnings. Kranot, the only one of the six that owns Palantir, added 3% to that stake. Palantir grew revenue 96% last quarter, against the 23% to 24% Palo Alto guides to for this fiscal year. Even so, Palantir trades at about 70x forward earnings, below Palo Alto's 76x.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock closed at $160.39 on November 16, 2026, down 20.5% from its October 21 close, and a fall that size tempts anyone who missed the climb. Palantir's chance of doubling from here depends on whether it keeps growing near the past year's pace. Doubling is not a stretch by the stock's own standards: after earlier drops this deep, its best price within a year stood a median 126.9% above its price on the day of the drop. But what did buyers of those earlier drops still hold a year later?

Palantir Stock Rose After Six Of Ten Drops

Since September 30, 2020, Palantir stock has had 12 drops like this one, each a fall of more than 20%. Ten of them now have a full year behind them. Across all ten, the stock's median gain twelve months later was 81.0%, and it was higher in six. All four losses came after the first four drops, in 2021 and 2022, while the six drops after them all ended the year higher. The two drops in January and June 2026 are too recent to judge.

Buyers usually had to sit through a further fall along the way. The stock's lowest close in the year after a drop was a median 20.1% below its price on the day of the drop. The best price came a median 263 days after the drop, close to nine months of waiting.

Palantir's Sales Nearly Doubled Over The Past Year

Palantir's revenue rose 87.1% to $7.29 billion over the four quarters to September 30, 2026. The September quarter alone grew 95.9% from a year earlier. Management said on the November 2 call that its U.S. commercial business grew 148% in that quarter.

The growth came with far more profit. Operating margin over the past four quarters was 45.6%, against 21.8% over the four quarters before. Palantir also ended September with $10.6 billion in cash and short-term investments, against $225 million of debt. Management raised its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to $8.53 billion, from $8.15 billion in August, though that is a forecast and not a result.

title: Palantir Raised Guidance 3 Times This Year. 1 Number Explains Why the Stock Fell.
detail:
Palantir Raised Guidance 3 Times This Year. 1 Number Explains Why the Stock Fell.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 7:03 AM CST 4 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) has been a successful long-term investment since its 2020 IPO. That's largely because it is also a successful business, as evidenced by its artificial intelligence platform, which has been widely adopted in both commercial and government settings. Palantir continues to outperform expectations, both externally and internally, and management has raised its annual guidance at every quarterly report this year.

It is often the case that raised guidance leads to an improved stock price, but this latest report was different. Palantir's stock price actually fell following its Q3 earnings, and the tech giant is now posting negative returns for the year.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why is that? I think one figure holds the clue.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Beating expectations has lost its luster

Every investor loves a good beat-and-raise quarter, but when that becomes the expectation, it loses its effectiveness. The market now expects Palantir to issue soft guidance each quarter and beat those expectations. After a while, this becomes the status quo for investors, and they demand bigger beats and raises because the original beat and raise have become the baseline.

But Palantir has another issue going on with its stock. While its growth rate was an impressive 96% year over year in Q3, the reality is that its stock has already priced in much of that growth. Shares also fell because of investor concerns about slowing growth in total contract value. The report was also released on a generally bad day for the market and got caught up in the sell-off.

Palantir is one of the most expensive stocks on the market, trading at over 100 times forward earnings and 68 times next year's earnings estimate. And that's even after this latest sell-off.

PLTR PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

You'd be hard-pressed to find another stock trading at that level in the AI realm, which puts Palantir in a class of its own. Sometimes being an outlier like this is a big problem, as it could lead to Palantir's valuation declining to a more reasonable level over the next year.

Most of Palantir's peers are trading at 20 to 40 times next year's earnings, which means that even if Palantir hits next year's expectations squarely, the stock would need to decline by at least 40% to be in a reasonable valuation range with its peers. That's the harsh reality of Palantir's stock, as so much growth is already priced in. This means investors may need to get used to underperformance for a while.

A Palantir sign displayed on an office building by Poetra_RH via Shutterstock

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock has declined more than 19% over the past month and is trading approximately 21% below its 52-week high. While the pullback reflects near-term valuation concerns and weak market sentiment toward AI-related stocks, it offers a buying opportunity for long-term investors, as PLTR's growth trajectory remains solid.

Palantir's outlook remains solid, led by strong demand across its U.S. commercial and government businesses. The acceleration in the adoption of its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) is strengthening its competitive positioning, driving enterprise customer engagement, and creating opportunities for sustained revenue expansion. Additionally, growing demand for Sovereign AI solutions could unlock a significant new growth avenue as governments and institutions increasingly prioritize secure, domestically controlled AI infrastructure.

Taken together, these growth drivers position Palantir to deliver solid revenue and earnings growth in the long term.

Palantir's Accelerating AIP Adoption Sets Stage for Solid Growth

Palantir's accelerating AIP adoption sets the stage for solid growth ahead. Its latest quarterly financial numbers suggest that this momentum could continue. Palantir reported a 96% year-over-year increase in revenue, with its U.S. business once again recording solid growth.

PLTR's domestic business revenue grew 119% year over year to $1.94 billion, highlighting strong demand in its largest market. Moreover, the acceleration in commercial activity suggests solid growth ahead.

U.S. commercial revenue stands out as the strongest growth driver. It surged 148% year over year to $984 million. U.S. commercial revenue led government revenue for the first time, supporting a more balanced revenue mix.

Customer growth and contract activity also support continued expansion. Palantir's U.S. commercial customer base increased 29% year over year to 686, indicating that adoption is spreading across a wider range of businesses. Meanwhile, commercial revenue grew 113% to $1.17 billion. Palantir secured $1.65 billion in commercial total contract value (TCV) bookings during the quarter, while U.S. commercial bookings reached $1.46 billion.

Another important growth opportunity lies in the emerging sovereign AI market. During the quarter, Palantir secured multiple eight-figure contracts as organizations accelerated their adoption of initial Sovereign AI capabilities. Although these agreements were shorter than the company's typical contracts, management expects their size and duration to increase as customers expand deployments and realize additional value from the technology. This creates an opportunity for Palantir to deepen existing relationships and generate larger, longer-term contracts as sovereign AI adoption matures.
